question: what is HRTF
gold_answer: Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound from a location in space; they depend on the size and shape of the head, ears and ear canal, so every person has a unique HRTF. Because measuring each user's is impractical, an HRTF for an average listener is used. A pair of HRTFs (both ears) can synthesise binaural sound and implement localisation in an XR system.

question: What is an IMU?
gold_answer: An inertial measurement unit is a composite hardware unit containing mainly a gyroscope (angular velocity), an accelerometer (linear acceleration on x, y, z) and a magnetometer (magnetic field strength on x, y, z); it is part of phones and HMDs. Tracking relies mainly on the gyroscope; accelerometer and magnetometer help detect and correct drift.

question: What is extended reality?
gold_answer: XR is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, covering all present or future immersive technologies such as AR, VR and MR; the X can be read as a variable whose values (A, V, M) give AR, VR, MR.

question: What is presence in VR?
gold_answer: Presence is the psychological (subjective) side: a state in which part or all of a person's experience is generated by or filtered through technology but the person's perception fails to acknowledge the technology's role (International Society for Presence Research definition); the user cannot distinguish the computer-generated stimuli from real-world ones. Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish virtual from real.

question: what is cybersicknes
gold_answer: Cybersickness (CS), also called visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect people interacting with VR; symptoms include nausea, headache, sweating, dry mouth, vomiting, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue and odd hand-eye coordination; it has many causes, not one.

question: What is vection?
gold_answer: Vection is the illusion (sensation) of self-motion: a person moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary gets visual input reporting motion while the balance sense/proprioception reports none, a sensory conflict; it is highest with motion in peripheral stimuli and linked to the onset and severity of cybersickness.

question: What is a frame buffer?
gold_answer: In a raster scan system the frame buffer is the video memory that stores the intensity values of all pixels, one memory location (a bit string) per pixel; its size equals the screen resolution.

question: Why are GPUs used for rendering in VR?
gold_answer: A GPU speeds up rendering because of its inherent parallel processing and the inherent parallelism of the rendering process, so it suits the complex scenes of realistic VR; CPUs are powerful but busy with other tasks, so GPU support is preferable (multi-GPU systems are typical). Lecture 58 adds that GPUs run transformation, lighting, projection, rasterisation, texturing and hidden-surface removal in parallel.

question: How does the Wizard of Oz approach work?
gold_answer: A prototyping technique: the participant believes they interact with an autonomous computer, but a hidden human operator (the wizard) produces the responses. Example: IBM's 1984 listening typewriter, where a hidden typist typed what the user spoke so the idea of speech recognition could be tested before the technology existed.

question: How does inside looking out infrared tracking work?
gold_answer: Infrared tracking uses targets that emit or reflect (infrared) light, easy to detect because they are bright; in the inside-looking-out configuration the camera is mounted on the user and detects external targets, from which it estimates the pose (in outside-looking-in, cameras in the environment see targets on the object).

question: What is the field of view and why does it matter for cybersickness?
gold_answer: FOV is the extent to which the headset display captures the user's field of vision (an angular measure of what can be seen). A larger FOV gives more immersion; reducing FOV can alleviate cybersickness, but an excessively narrow FOV lowers immersion and increases head movement, which may worsen cybersickness, so an optimal FOV is needed; FOV adjustment is a developer-side mitigation.

question: Why is a mouse-driven CAD system not a virtual reality system?
gold_answer: A VR system must have all three characteristics: virtual environment, immersive experience through the senses, and interaction. A CAD system has a virtual environment and interaction (via the mouse) but no immersion: the user sees the real world around the screen. So it is not VR.

question: Why does reducing cybersickness involve a trade-off?
gold_answer: Mitigation strategies often affect presence, the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience, so reducing cybersickness must be balanced against preserving the experience; complete prevention is generally not possible.

question: Why did the Majuli VR tour store its videos in the cloud for the Oculus Quest 2 version?
gold_answer: The Quest 2 is a standalone device with less computing power and storage than a workstation, so the app had to be smaller; videos take the most space, so they were stored in the cloud and loaded on selection, cutting the app to 5.1 GB and the computation; the cost is a need for high bandwidth, network coverage and low latency.

question: What is the difference between immersion and presence?
gold_answer: Immersion is the technological, objective side: the degree to which a VR system projects stimuli onto the senses (extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, plot-informing). Presence is the psychological, subjective side: perceiving the virtual as real. Immersion can aid and limit presence but does not ensure it.

question: What is the difference between AR and VR?
gold_answer: AR alters (enhances) the ongoing perception of the real world with registered digital content; VR completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment. VR does not need the place to exist physically; AR/MR needs the real place.

question: How do full gait, partial gait and gait negation locomotion techniques differ?
gold_answer: All three are walking-based locomotion. Full gait: the user really walks (within a limited physical space) and the walk is translated to virtual movement, the most natural. Partial gait: the user walks in place, using devices such as pressure mats/sensors. Gait negation: a special setup (linear treadmill, motorised floor tiles, human-sized hamster ball, friction-free platform) cancels lateral movement and keeps the user's position fixed.

question: What is the difference between inside-out and outside-in tracking?
gold_answer: Categorised by where the sensors are. Outside-in: the user's device has no trackers; external sensors (cameras, markers) in the room track the user, so it only works within that area (most VR headsets using external sensors). Inside-out: cameras/sensors are on the device (e.g. the HMD), no external devices, no area restriction (e.g. HoloLens, Intel Project Alloy, Qualcomm VR820).

question: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical prototypes?
gold_answer: A horizontal prototype shows the whole interface at the surface (look, feel, appearance) with no functionality, good for discussing appearance; a vertical prototype implements a few selected, commonly used features in depth (first to last screen), good for analysing interactions.

question: How is a within-subject design different from a between-subject design?
gold_answer: Within-subject (repeated measures): every participant does the tasks of all test conditions; easier to manage but suffers from the practice effect (reduced by randomising or varying task order). Between-subject: the tasks for the conditions are divided among subsets of participants; may be forced by participant/resource availability.

question: How do vector scan and raster scan displays differ?
gold_answer: Vector (random) scan devices treat an image as continuous primitives (lines, curves) and excite only the pixels on them; they need high precision and are costly, used in specialised settings. Raster scan devices treat the image as the whole pixel grid and excite all pixels in sequence (left to right, top to bottom); they need less precision, are much cheaper, and are used in commercial devices (phones, TVs).

question: What are the five stages of contextual inquiry?
gold_answer: Plan, initiate, execute, close and reflect (in that order): plan the goals and arrangements; initiate by getting permissions and putting users at ease; execute the observation and recording; close with thanks; reflect by analysing the data (affinity diagram) to identify design goals.

question: What are the causes of cybersickness?
gold_answer: Many factors. Internal (user) factors such as age and gender; external factors: hardware (display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, input technology) and VR content (visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration of exposure, visual complexity); underlying sensory mismatch (e.g. vection).

question: What are the three fidelities in VR design?
gold_answer: Representational fidelity (how far the experience conveys familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth), interaction fidelity (how far the physical actions for a virtual task match those of the real task), and experiential fidelity (how far the user's personal experience matches the creator's intended experience); developers should keep them high to avoid the uncanny valley.

question: What are the six qualities of immersion?
gold_answer: Extensive (range of sensory modalities), matching (congruence between modalities, e.g. head movement and view), surrounding (panoramic cues, e.g. wide FOV), vivid (energy within a modality: resolution, lighting, frame rate), interactive (user can change the world and get responses) and plot-informing (a consistent scripted story) — from Slater and Wilbur's definition.

question: How is the System Usability Scale (SUS) score calculated?
gold_answer: Ten statements rated 1-5. S = 2.5 x ( sum over odd statements of (r_i - 1) + sum over even statements of (5 - r_i) ). The score reads as a percentage; 70 or more is desirable.

question: What formula is used for drift correction when combining gyroscope and camera orientations?
gold_answer: theta_d(k) = alpha * theta_g(k) + (1 - alpha) * theta_c(k): theta_g from integrating the gyroscope, theta_c from the camera, theta_d the drift-corrected orientation, alpha a gain between 0 and 1.

question: In the simple lighting model, how is the light intensity reaching the viewer computed?
gold_answer: As the sum I = I_amb + I_diff + I_spec. Ambient = Ka x ambient intensity; diffuse = Kd x Is x (N . L) when N . L > 0 else 0; specular (Phong) = Ks x Is x (V . r)^Ns when V . r > 0 else 0, with r = 2(L . N)N - L; coefficients Ka, Kd, Ks in 0..1.

question: How is the perceived visual speed computed in the natural walking model for a VR tour?
gold_answer: v_visual = g x v_actual, with visual gain g typically 2.10; v_actual = f(x) x 0.157 x (h x 1.72)^2, f(x) the instantaneous step frequency (a Fourier-series slow-in-slow-out pattern) and h the user's height.

question: Which statistical test should I use for a within-subject design with one factor at two levels?
gold_answer: Parametric: the paired sample t-test; non-parametric: the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (and McNemar's test if the measure is nominal/categorical).

gold_answer: Lecture 28 (Visual Perception & Displays II), around 14:25: stereoscopy with binocular vision (from 11:44). Its history (Wheatstone 1838, Brewster 1860) is in lecture 6 around 4:20.

gold_answer: Lecture 39 (and 38): the three interaction types in immersive design (object interaction, navigation, system control) and object interaction = selection and manipulation; lecture 40 covers the remaining two.

question: What is lecture 36 for?
gold_answer: Lecture 36 (Usability requirement gathering and specification) explains how contextual inquiry and affinity diagram analysis support usability requirement gathering: modes and master-apprentice model, the five stages, affinity diagrams (note-taking and calendar examples) to derive requirement categories and design recommendations.

question: What are the six modules of this course?
gold_answer: From lecture 63: (1) introduction (lectures 1-12), (2) XR hardware and software incl. tracking (13-22), (3) human factors (23-31), (4) building XR systems: development life cycle, Majuli case study, requirements, design, implementation (32-48), (5) optimisation: experience (49-53) and resource (54-59), (6) linking theory to practice and concluding remarks (60-63).

question: Why do the cybersickness-reduction techniques that restrict the field of view work on the edges of the view rather than the centre?
gold_answer: Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement (lecture 27). Vection, the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli and correlates positively with visual motion stimulus, so visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cybersickness (lecture 11). Restricting the field of view therefore reduces peripheral optical flow and ideally reduces cybersickness; an asymmetric mask obscures only peripheral regions with higher optical flow during locomotion and leaves low-flow regions visible (lecture 12). The cost is that field-of-view restriction can reduce presence and impair visual tasks (lecture 12).

question: Why did the Majuli VR tour move users between places with teleportation and a vehicle instead of letting them walk everywhere?
gold_answer: Free walking is the most natural travel technique but completely free walking is not practical; full-gait walking is confined to the physical space and mapped to a potentially infinite virtual space, with a mismatch (lecture 40). Teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic walking, and teleportation instead of steering is a listed locomotion modification for cybersickness (lectures 11, 12). In the Majuli design the island's geographic spread is large and content rich, so exploring it by walking takes a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness; a virtual vehicle metaphor (a pre-planned route, the user selects a destination) was added for long-distance travel, with controlled joystick navigation without abrupt movements, while the vehicle's viewpoint speed must be chosen carefully (lecture 41). Teleportation gives the shortest exposure but is not natural (lecture 51), so the tour combines walking within each information point with teleportation or the vehicle between points because one technique alone would not suit the large spread (lecture 59).

question: How does the finding that longer VR exposure makes people sicker turn into a method for planning a tour route?
gold_answer: Prolonged exposure through HMDs leads to greater cybersickness (lecture 11), and users are advised to avoid long continuous exposure, with roughly 55 to 70 minutes suggested as generally safe (lecture 12). The optimisation lectures therefore try to control exposure duration, which depends on world size, travelling speed, travel time and interaction time (lecture 51). The first approach represents the tour as a graph of points of interest and finds the path covering all of them in minimum time with a travelling salesman formulation using a natural walking-speed model (lecture 51). If that minimum still exceeds the time threshold above which cybersickness may occur (walking a whole satra could take up to a day), a second approach assigns each point an importance and waiting time and finds the most important path within the threshold with a vehicle-routing-with-profit solver (lectures 52, 53).

question: Which headsets, development tools and computers did the Majuli VR tour use, and how did the limits of those devices shape the app?
gold_answer: The tour was built in Unity (version 2021.3.22f1) for the Oculus Quest 2 and for Android smartphones (Android 6), using the XR toolkit for the Quest version and the Google VR SDK for the Cardboard version (lecture 44); Unity is a cross-platform engine supporting over 20 platforms (lecture 60). The evaluation used a Meta Quest 2 (1920 by 1832 pixels per eye) connected to a Windows 11 PC with a GTX 1080 GPU via Oculus Link, with joystick-based controllers (lecture 47). The Quest 2 is a standalone device with its own processor and memory but less computing power and storage than a high-end graphics workstation, so all videos were stored in the cloud, giving a 5.1 GB app that needs high bandwidth, network coverage and low latency (lectures 44, 59). For smartphones in Cardboard, images were compressed and most videos removed, cutting the size from about 10 GB to 0.7 GB at the cost of realism (lectures 44, 59).

question: What different ways can an XR system track the user, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of each?
gold_answer: Head tracking is the most important thing to track in VR (lecture 13); full-body tracking can use several surrounding cameras that see reflective markers on a suit (lecture 14). By sensor position, outside-in tracking uses external sensors or markers and is restricted to the area where they are placed, whereas inside-out tracking carries the sensors with the user and works anywhere (lecture 16). Inertial tracking in an IMU relies mainly on the gyroscope, which drifts, so drift correction needs at least two sensors blended, for example a gyroscope with a camera, accelerometer or magnetometer using a gain parameter alpha (lecture 17). Other tracker families are electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic, vision-based (infrared tracking is unaffected by poor lighting and shadows), inertial and hybrid; SLAM gives drift-free tracking of unknown environments, and GPS tracks position outdoors but is less accurate indoors (lecture 18).

question: What can developers, designers and users do to reduce cybersickness, from the headset to the design of a whole tour?
gold_answer: Developer-side strategies are field-of-view adjustment (which reduces peripheral optical flow but can reduce presence), dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations such as phantom legs, floor vibrations and modified motion platforms, and locomotion changes such as teleportation instead of steering; users can limit continuous exposure (about 55 to 70 minutes), habituate with repeated short exposures, use slow diaphragmatic breathing, and use pleasant music and air flow (lecture 12). The cybersickness guidelines are VR-specific design guidelines and may not apply to AR (lecture 38). The Majuli design used controlled joystick navigation without abrupt movement and a vehicle metaphor whose viewpoint speed must be chosen carefully (lecture 41). The optimisation lectures reduce exposure duration with a minimum-time path and, if that exceeds the cybersickness time threshold, a most-important-points path within the threshold (lectures 51, 52, 53).

question: What does Unity's render pipeline support build on from earlier in the course?
gold_answer: The Unity lectures aim at support for the graphics pipeline discussed earlier (object definition, scene construction, lighting, view transformation, scan conversion) so a developer need not implement it (lecture 60). The earlier pipeline has five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, viewing transformation and scan conversion (lecture 55); Unity's model files carry the object definition as meshes, the popular mesh representation of lecture 55, plus materials and textures (lecture 61). Lighting from lecture 56 is supported by Unity lights and shadows (lecture 61), and the camera set-up of the viewing stage in lecture 57 is done in Unity by adding a camera, after which Unity does the other calculations (lecture 61). Scan conversion and rendering with GPUs and graphics libraries (lecture 58) are handled by Unity through native libraries such as DirectX, Metal, OpenGL and Vulkan (lecture 61).

question: What earlier ideas does the evaluation of the Majuli VR tour rest on?
gold_answer: Presence is a psychological state of being in the virtual environment, distinct from immersion (lecture 8), and cybersickness is measured with questionnaires such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire with 16 items in three subscales (lecture 11; lecture 44 repeats SSQ as the most used cybersickness questionnaire). The evaluation uses the empirical-study process of research question, variables, controlled experiment (lecture 45) and experiment design with representative participants, 12 to 25 generally being enough (lecture 46). The three user categories identified in the design, pilgrims, students and tourists (lecture 41), were the groups of the 27 participants (lecture 47). It measured presence with the QEP questionnaire and cybersickness with the SSQ before and after exposure, finding good presence and a significant pre-post change only in oculomotor and total sickness (lecture 47).

question: What earlier ideas does the resource optimisation of the Majuli app for the Quest 2 and phones rest on?
gold_answer: The hardware lecture says a VR system's processing element is typically a PC or a high-end workstation with a good GPU, useful for rendering complex scenes (lecture 14). The human factors lecture says VR needs frame rates much higher than the 24 or 60 fps of television and film, and the resource lecture notes a higher refresh rate is preferable (lectures 28, 54); VR is resource hungry and the aim is a good experience on affordable hardware (lecture 54). Interactive VR redraws the scene with every input and anti-aliasing adds further computation, so rendering cost grows manifold and GPUs exploit the parallelism (lecture 58). Hence the Quest 2, with less compute and storage than a workstation and about 10 GB of rich content, needed cloud storage for videos (with bandwidth, coverage and latency demands), and phones needed compressed images, no video and in extreme cases removed features (lecture 59).

question: How are presence and cybersickness related in this course, and when does reducing one cost the other?
gold_answer: Control over motion affects presence directly and cybersickness indirectly through presence; greater presence generally leads to lower cybersickness, though not always (lecture 11). A sensory mismatch can cause cybersickness for some users, and when the user consciously notices the conflict presence is compromised (lecture 26). Mitigation is a trade-off: restricting the field of view reduces cybersickness but can reduce presence (lecture 12), so mitigation must avoid compromising presence (lecture 49). The Majuli evaluation measured both, presence with the QEP questionnaire and cybersickness with the SSQ before and after exposure, finding good presence but significant changes in oculomotor and total sickness (lecture 47).

question: How can a smartphone in a cardboard box give a 3D headset experience, and what did the Majuli tour give up in its Cardboard version?
gold_answer: In stereoscopy each eye views its own image at the same time and the brain combines the left and right images into a 3D view, aided by binocular vision (lecture 28). A cardboard housing holds a smartphone, and if the phone displays stereoscopic views, wearing it as a headset gives an immersive environment without an expensive headset; it costs only about 500 to 1000 rupees (lecture 59). The Majuli Cardboard version used Unity with the Google VR SDK on Android 6 (lecture 44). To fit phones the images were compressed and most videos removed, shrinking the app to 0.7 GB from roughly 10 GB, which made the experience less realistic than the full version (lectures 44, 59).

question: Why might adding vibration or motion cues to a VR setup reduce cybersickness?
gold_answer: Motion sickness occurs when the brain receives conflicting signals from different senses, with symptoms similar to cybersickness (lecture 10). In vection, vision reports that the user is moving or accelerating while the balance sense and proprioception say the user is motionless, and the goal should be to balance the experience across senses (lecture 26). The mitigation lecture lists hardware-level alterations that add matching cues: phantom legs (haptic cues synchronised to footsteps, reduced cybersickness to a great extent), floor vibrations matching the virtual environment, sound with vibration, and modified motion platforms where short bursts of rotational acceleration matched visual forward acceleration and were quite effective (lecture 12). The hardware lecture presents haptics and motion platforms, which move the whole body to give a sense of physical motion and gravity, as VR output devices (lecture 14).
